Question 1

Let's take a look at this example of rampant referential phrasing:

Ginny had hoped to spend her vacation scouring the indigenous markets for Ecuadorian textiles.They are known to be excellent sites for acquiring unique fabrics and, since it was planned to last two weeks, she had more than enough time for the task.

Check out the bolded words. What are they doing in the sentences?

Correct!

The bolded words refer to concepts introduced earlier in the stimulus.

The LSAT uses referential phrasing to make stimuli more wordy and confusing. Unless you translate out the referential phrasing as you go, it can be very difficult to keep the ideas in the stimulus straight.

Ginny had hoped to spend her [Ginny's] vacation scouring the indigenous markets for Ecuadorian textiles. They[the markets] are known to be excellent sites for acquiring unique fabrics and, since it [the vacation] was planned to last two weeks, she [Ginny] had more than enough time for the task [shopping].

What do these bolded words refer to?

Ginny, who had grown up on a farm and was no stranger to the outdoors, had been looking forward to hiking the Andes. Her husband Omar, ever concerned about his hair, was less enthused about the activity. He had grown up in the city and was less inclined to outdoorsy activities than she but being the longest continental range in the world they were a must.

A

Ginny / vacationing / Omar / Ginny / farming

B

Ginny / hiking the Andes / Omar / Ginny / the Andes

C

Ginny / farming / Omar / Ginny / hiking
